lead: Continuous media such as audio and video must be produced on time, not merely soon. The operating system (OS) therefore schedules CPU, disk and input/output (I/O) against deadlines. This is real-time scheduling, not fairness. A video call on a phone, a streaming box and a classroom lecture capture all depend on it. Only a few universities teach this topic. The main model gives each task a period, an execution time and a deadline; from these you compute utilisation and test a scheduling policy.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the layered pipeline and Chapter 6.5 for the QoS promises.

sections.h3: Real-time task model and CPU scheduling tests

blocks.text: Each periodic task i has period T_i (time between releases, ms), execution time C_i (CPU time needed, ms) and deadline D_i, often equal to T_i. Utilisation is U = Σ C_i/T_i; n is task count, and C_i/T_i is the fraction of CPU task i demands. A set is schedulable if a policy can meet every deadline.

Rate-monotonic (RM) scheduling is fixed priority: shorter period gets higher priority. For n tasks the sufficient RM utilisation bound is U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1). At n = 3 this is 3(2^(1/3) − 1) = 0.7798. Earliest-deadline-first (EDF) is dynamic: the ready task with the earliest deadline runs. For preemptive periodic tasks with D_i = T_i, EDF is schedulable exactly when U ≤ 1. Both tests assume preemption and no blocking.
U = Σ (C_i ÷ T_i) ≤ 1 for EDF; for RM, U ≤ n(2^(1/n) − 1)
blocks.where: C_i is execution time of task i in ms; T_i is its period in ms; n is the number of periodic tasks; U is CPU utilisation.

blocks.text: Continuous media also need disk and I/O deadlines. A media file is stored in contiguous blocks or large extents so a request needs few seeks; random small blocks waste head movement. Disk scheduling has two useful policies. SCAN sweeps the head from one end to the other, serving requests in track order. EDF-for-disk serves the pending request with the earliest deadline, even if the head must move farther. SCAN gives good throughput; disk EDF protects playout deadlines. Double buffering plays buffer A while buffer B fills, then swaps them. Read-ahead fetches the next blocks before they are needed. Resource reservation admits a new stream only if CPU, disk bandwidth and network share remain. Priority inversion happens when a low-priority thread holds a lock needed by a video thread, and a medium-priority thread preempts the holder. The video thread waits although it has higher priority. Priority inheritance lets the holder run at the waiter's priority until it releases the lock.

figure.caption: At three tasks the rate-monotonic bound is about 0.78, so a task set at 0.9 is safe under EDF but not guaranteed under RM.

spec.aria: A plot of the rate-monotonic utilisation bound falling from 1 toward 0.69 as the number of tasks grows, with a flat EDF line at 1 and a line at U = 0.9 for the example.

examples.question: Three periodic tasks share one CPU. Audio runs 4 ms every 10 ms; video runs 10 ms every 40 ms; network runs 5 ms every 20 ms. (a) Find total utilisation U. (b) State whether EDF guarantees all deadlines. (c) Compute the RM bound for three tasks and compare.
steps: Read periods and execution times: audio C1 = 4 ms, T1 = 10 ms; video C2 = 10 ms, T2 = 40 ms; network C3 = 5 ms, T3 = 20 ms.
Compute each share: audio 4/10 = 0.40; video 10/40 = 0.25; network 5/20 = 0.25.
EDF test for D_i = T_i: 0.90 ≤ 1, so EDF guarantees every deadline.
Compare: 0.90 > 0.7798, so the RM sufficient test fails; RM may still work but the bound cannot guarantee it.
examples.answer: U = 0.90; EDF guarantees all deadlines; RM bound = 0.7798, so RM alone cannot guarantee every deadline.
examples.check:
a = 4/10
v = 10/40
n = 5/20
U = a + v + n
rm = 3*((2**(1/3))-1)
print(round(U, 2))
print(round(rm, 4))

traps: Using n = 2 when three tasks are present: the RM bound is 0.8284 for n = 2, not 0.7798 for n = 3.
Treating U ≤ 1 as an RM test. It is the exact EDF test for D_i = T_i; the RM sufficient bound is lower.
Forgetting preemption: both tests assume a higher-priority or earlier-deadline task can interrupt the running task.
Mixing CPU EDF with disk EDF: CPU picks by deadline among runnable tasks; disk picks by deadline among pending I/O requests, and head position still matters for SCAN.
Calling priority inversion a deadline miss: the miss is the symptom; inversion is a low-priority lock holder blocking a high-priority thread.

quiz.q: Define period, execution time and CPU utilisation for a periodic task.
quiz.a: Period T is time between releases; execution time C is CPU time per release; utilisation contribution is C/T.

quiz.q: Why can EDF use U ≤ 1 while RM uses a lower bound?
quiz.a: EDF always runs the earliest deadline, so the exact test is U ≤ 1. RM has fixed priorities by period, so its simple test is sufficient but not exact.

quiz.q: Tasks have C/T = 2/8, 3/12 and 5/20. Compute U and state whether EDF is safe.
A video thread misses deadlines only when a backup process runs. Explain priority inversion and give one fix.
quiz.a: A low-priority thread holds a lock the video thread needs; a medium-priority backup thread preempts the holder, so the video thread waits. Use priority inheritance: the holder runs at the video thread's priority until it releases the lock.

quiz.q: Compute the RM bound for n = 4 tasks.
What is double buffering in media playback?
quiz.a: Two buffers alternate: one is played while the other is filled, hiding refill time.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real-time OS support appears in Android audio, automotive infotainment, IPTV set-top boxes and video conferencing. Search 'rate-monotonic analysis', 'earliest deadline first', 'Linux deadline scheduling', 'priority inheritance' and 'disk scheduling for continuous media'.
